                                                                              1

The lecture begins with the transition from pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, which links
glycolysis to mitochondrial oxidative metabolism.
We will then follow acetyl-CoA through the TCA cycle, focusing on where carbon is lost
as CO₂ and where energy is captured as NADH, FADH₂, and GTP.
The cycle is highly regulated according to the energy state of the cell. High ATP and
NADH generally suppress pathway activity, while low-energy signals such as ADP and
Ca²⁺ can stimulate key regulatory enzymes.
The TCA cycle also has an important biosynthetic role. Intermediates can leave the
cycle and contribute to synthesis of fatty acids, amino acids, heme, and glucose-related
pathways. Because the cycle participates in both breakdown and synthesis, it is
described as amphibolic
Finally, when TCA intermediates are withdrawn for biosynthesis, they must be
replenished. This is the role of anaplerotic reactions, especially the conversion of
pyruvate to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase.
Transcription:
-  The Krebs cycle has many different names. It’s also called the TCA cycle and the
   citric acid cycle.
-  We’re going to follow the journey of pyruvate and see how it gets converted to
   acetyl-CoA. This is what we call a link reaction.





                                                                              2

-  Then, acetyl-CoA will enter the Krebs cycle, or the TCA cycle, and we’re going to see
  how the carbons are lost as CO2. and how energy is captured as NADH, FADH2 , and
  GTP
-  The Krebs cycle has two important roles:
     o  It helps us produce energy
     o  It has very important biosynthetic roles because intermediates of the Krebs
          cycle can leave the cycle and contribute to biosynthesis.
- We can make important molecules from these intermediates, whether they are
  amino acids, heme, and importantly glucose.
-  The Krebs cycle is both anabolic and catabolic, so we describe it as amphibolic.
-  There are also anaplerotic reactions that replace important intermediates of the
  Krebs cycle to keep the cycle going.
-  Reads the objectives





                                                                              2

Glycolysis ends in the cytosol with formation of pyruvate. For pyruvate to contribute to
mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, it must first be converted into acetyl-CoA.
This reaction is catalyzed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, PDH, in the
mitochondrial matrix. During the reaction, one carbon is released as CO₂, and NAD⁺ is
reduced to NADH.
The acetyl-CoA produced then enters the TCA cycle, where its two-carbon acetyl group
is oxidized further. The cycle captures energy mainly in the form of NADH and FADH₂,
which later contribute to ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation.
Key point: Glycolysis and the TCA cycle are linked by the conversion of pyruvate to
acetyl-CoA.
Transcription:
-  Before going into details of the krebs cycle, we need to study the link reaction,
  which converts pyruvate to acetyl-coA





                                                                              3

Pyruvate is produced in the cytosol, but both pyruvate dehydrogenase and pyruvate
carboxylase are located in the mitochondrial matrix.
The outer mitochondrial membrane is relatively permeable to small metabolites
through porins. The inner mitochondrial membrane is much more selective.
Pyruvate therefore crosses the inner membrane through the mitochondrial pyruvate
carrier, MPC.
Once inside the matrix, pyruvate has two important metabolic fates that we will use in
this lecture:
PyruvateAcetyl-CoA
through the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle;
and
Pyruvate Oxaloacetate
through pyruvate carboxylase, which is important for anaplerosis and
gluconeogenesis.
Key point: pyruvate cannot simply diffuse across the inner mitochondrial membrane;
transport through MPC is required
Transcription:
-  The enzymes for converting pyruvate, whether we are converting it to acetyl-CoA or
   to oxaloacetate, are located in the mitochondria.





                                                                              4

-  Pyruvate first needs to cross the outer mitochondrial membrane. It can cross with
  the help of porins, which allow the entry of small molecules such as pyruvate.
-  The inner mitochondrial membrane is more selective, so we need a carrier called
  the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier.
-  The mitochondrial pyruvate carrier transports pyruvate inside the mitochondria.
-  Once inside the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate has two important fates:
     o  It can be converted to acetyl-CoA through the pyruvate dehydrogenase
         complex, which we will study next
     o  It can be converted to oxaloacetate, which we will discuss toward the end of
         the lecture





                                                                              4

The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex connects cytosolic glycolysis with
mitochondrial acetyl-CoA metabolism.
Pyruvate contains three carbons. During the PDH reaction, one carbon is removed as
CO₂. The remaining two-carbon fragment is oxidized and transferred to coenzyme A,
producing acetyl-CoA.
At the same time, NAD⁺ accepts electrons and is reduced to NADH.
The reaction is therefore an oxidative decarboxylation:
decarboxylation because CO₂ is removed
oxidation because electrons are removed from the pyruvate-derived carbon fragment
PDH is an effectively irreversible metabolic step, so it is an important point controlling
entry of carbohydrate-derived carbon into acetyl-CoA metabolism.
Because one glucose produces two pyruvate molecules, PDH operates twice per
glucose, yielding 2 acetyl-CoA, 2 CO₂, and 2 NADH.
The PDH complex itself contains three core enzyme activities, which we will introduce
together with its required coenzymes on the next slide.
Transcription:
- We havent started the krebs cycle yet. We’re studying the reaction that converts
   pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, and the enzyme is pyruvate dehydrogenase.
-  The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex connects glycolysis with the Krebs cycle.





                                                                              5

-  Pyruvate has three carbons. During the PDH reaction, one carbon is removed as
  CO2, and the remaining two carbons are oxidized and transferred to coA, producing
   acetyl-CoA.
-  In the link reaction, three things happen
     o We remove the carboxyl group from pyruvate as CO2
     o We oxidize pyruvate by transferring electrons to NAD+ forming NADH
     o We add a CoA group to the remaining two carbons to from acetyl-CoA
-  This reaction is irreversible and is an important control point for the entry of
   carbohydrate-derived carbon into acetyl-CoA metabolism.
- One glucose produces two pyruvate molecules so this reaction yields:
          -  2 acetyl-CoA
          -  2 CO2
          -  2 NADH
- PDH complex is a very complex enzyme because its doing three reactions:
   decarboxylation, oxidation, and adding a CoA group.





                                                                              5

The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is a multienzyme complex that requires five
coenzymes to complete the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
TLCFN : mnemonic The Lovely Coenzymes For Nerds
TPP, derived from thiamine or vitamin B1, participates in the initial decarboxylation of
pyruvate.
Lipoamide or lipoic acid acts as a flexible carrier within the complex, transferring both
the acetyl group and reducing equivalents between enzyme components.
Coenzyme A, derived from vitamin B5, accepts the acetyl group to form acetyl-CoA.
FAD, derived from vitamin B2, participates in reoxidizing the reduced lipoamide arm.
Finally, NAD⁺, derived from vitamin B3, accepts electrons and is reduced to NADH.
The five-cofactor requirement explains why deficiencies affecting some B vitamins,
especially thiamine, can impair oxidative metabolism.
Key point: PDH is not a single enzyme acting alone; it is a coordinated complex that
depends on multiple cofactors to carry out oxidative decarboxylation.
Transcription:
- PDH requires 5 coenzymes, or helpers, to assist it in this complex step
-  These coenzymes are mostly derived from vitamins, specifically B vitamins
-  The mnemonic is “ The lovely co-enzyme for nerds”
-  These coenzymes are derived from vitamins B1, B2, B3, and B5. Lipoic acid is not





                                                                              6

-  derived from a vitamin.
1. TPP (thiamine phosphatase) is derived from B1
     o   Its very important, B1 deficiency causes many disturbance specifically in the
          nervous system.
     o  Function: required for decarboxylation of pyruvate
2.  Lipoic acid is not derived from a vitamin
     o  Function: transfers the acetyl group
3. CoA is derived from B5
     o  Function: accepts the acetyl group
4. FAD is derived from B2
     o  Function: accepts electrons and becomes FADH2
5. NAD+ is derived from B3 (niacin)
     o  Function: final electron acceptor; becomes NADH + H
-  This is the summary of the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction, which converts
   pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
- We need five coenzymes to help the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.





                                                                              6

Thiamine, or vitamin B1, is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate, TPP.
TPP is an essential cofactor for several oxidative decarboxylation reactions, including
pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Therefore, thiamine
deficiency impairs both the entry of pyruvate into acetyl-CoA metabolism and an
important step within the TCA cycle itself.
When PDH activity falls, pyruvate cannot be efficiently converted to acetyl-CoA. More
pyruvate is therefore available for conversion to lactate, which can contribute to
hyperlactatemia and, in severe cases, lactic acidosis.
Reduced PDH and TCA activity also decrease ATP generation. Tissues with high energy
requirements, particularly the brain, are therefore especially vulnerable.
Clinically, thiamine deficiency is important in patients with malnutrition or chronic
alcohol use, and severe deficiency can cause Wernicke encephalopathy.
n clinical practice, patients at risk of thiamine deficiency — especially those with
chronic alcohol use, malnutrition, or prolonged poor intake — are generally given
thiamine before or together with glucose. The reason is that glucose metabolism
increases thiamine utilization, which may worsen the neurologic manifestations of
Wernicke encephalopathy if thiamine stores are already depleted.
Transcription:
-  Vitamin B1 is the precursor for TPP, which is one of the five coenzymes required for





                                                                              7

-  pyruvate dehydrogenase
-  TPP is also required for alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, one of the enzymes of
  the krebs cycle
-   If thiamine is deficient, PDH activity will go down. As a result, pyruvate will
  accumulate, leading to the accumulation of lactate.
-  This leads to reduced ATP production and may increase the risk of lactic acidosis
-  Thiamine deficiency can manifest as neurological disturbances. If its very severe, it
  can lead to Wernicke encephalopathy.
-  Causes of thiamine deficiency:
     o Malnutrition
     o Eating disorders
     o Chronic alcoholism
-  These patients are at risk of having thiamine deficiency
-  Treatment of thiamine deficiency:
     o  If you have a patient with severe thiamine deficiency, you have to give them
        an injection of thiamine intravenously
     o You administer it along with glucose because you cannot give them glucose
          alone. You have to give them glucose and thiamine
     o  If you give them glucose first, this will worsen the symptoms of thiamine
          deficiency because glucose metabolism requires thiamine.





                                                                              7

Pyruvate dehydrogenase is regulated mainly by reversible phosphorylation.
When PDH is phosphorylated, it is inactive. This phosphorylation is carried out by PDH
kinase.
When the phosphate is removed by PDH phosphatase, PDH becomes active again.
A high-energy state, characterized by increased ATP, NADH, and acetyl-CoA,
suppresses PDH activity. This prevents unnecessary oxidation of pyruvate when the cell
already has adequate energy.
In contrast, when energy demand rises, ADP and NAD⁺ increase, favoring pyruvate
oxidation.
In contracting muscle, increased Ca²⁺ activates PDH phosphatase, which activates PDH
so that more acetyl-CoA can enter the TCA cycle and support ATP production.
Key point:
PDH phosphorylation = OFF
PDH dephosphorylation = ON
Transcription:
-  Pyruvate dehydrogenase is regulated by phosphorylation
-   If the enzyme is phosphorylated with the help of PDH kinase, it becomes inactive.
-   If it is dephosphorylated by a phosphatase, it becomes active.
- When energy is abundant :





                                                                              8

o High energy is reflected by increased ATP, increased NADH, and increased
         acetyl-CoA
     o  All these three factors activate the kinase enzyme, leading to
         phosphorylation of PDH and making it inactive
     o Therefore, less pyruvate will enter acetyl-CoA metabolism
- When energy demand is high :
     o Low energy status is reflected by increased ADP, increased NAD+, and
          increased calcium in contracting muscle
     o The phosphatase will be activated
     o The phosphatase removes the phosphate group, making PDH active
     o Therefore, more pyruvate will be converted to acetyl-CoA
- Summary: PDH activity is highly regulated by the energy level of the cell.
Phosphorylation switches PDH off, and dephosphorylation turns it on.





                                                                              8

The TCA cycle, also called the citric acid cycle or Krebs cycle, occurs mainly in the
mitochondrial matrix.
The cycle begins when a 2-carbon acetyl group from acetyl-CoA combines with 4-
carbon oxaloacetate to form 6-carbon citrate.
As the cycle proceeds, the acetyl-derived carbon is oxidized and energy is captured
primarily in reduced electron carriers:
3NADH + 1 FADH 2 + 1 GTP
and 2 CO₂ are released per turn.
The cycle ends by regenerating oxaloacetate, which can combine with another acetyl-
CoA and begin another turn.
The TCA cycle itself produces only a small amount of direct high-energy phosphate as
GTP. Most of its ATP yield comes later, when NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to
the electron transport chain.
Key point: the main role of the TCA cycle is to capture energy from acetyl-CoA in
NADH and FADH₂, while regenerating oxaloacetate.
Transcription:
-   The link reaction connects glycolysis to the Krebs cycle.
-   The Krebs cycle has three names: the TCA cycle, citric acid cycle, and Krebs cycle.
-     It occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.





                                                                              9

-     It begins when the two-carbon acetyl group from acetyl-CoA combines with the
    four-carbon oxaloacetate.
-   When acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate, it forms the six-carbon citrate.
-   As the cycle proceeds, carbons are released as CO₂.
-  We release two CO₂ per cycle and capture energy in the form of electron carriers,
   NADH and FADH₂, as well as GTP.
-   Products per one acetyl-CoA molecule
3 NADH
1 FADH₂
1 GTP
2 CO₂
-    This is a total of 10 ATP equivalents per acetyl-CoA molecule.
-      If you compare this to glycolysis, you will see that we are producing much more
    energy here than we did in glycolysis.
-  We go from six-carbon citrate to five-carbon alpha-ketoglutarate, then to four-
    carbon succinyl-CoA, succinate, fumarate, and malate.
-   At the end, we regenerate oxaloacetate. That’s why we call it a cycle, because we
    produce oxaloacetate at the end, which is also needed for the first reaction.





                                                                              9

The TCA cycle consists of eight enzyme-catalyzed reactions.
The cycle begins when 2-carbon acetyl-CoA combines with 4-carbon oxaloacetate to
produce 6-carbon citrate.
Two oxidative decarboxylation reactions then reduce the carbon number:
isocitrate, 6C → α-ketoglutarate, 5C
α-ketoglutarate, 5C → succinyl-CoA, 4C
These are the two steps where CO₂ is released.
Energy is captured at several points:
Step 3 produces NADH
Step 4 produces NADH
Step 5 produces GTP
Step 6 produces FADH₂
Step 8 produces NADH
At the end of Step 8, oxaloacetate is regenerated, allowing another acetyl-CoA to
enter the cycle.
Students do not need to treat all eight reactions as equally important. We will focus
next on the steps that are most important for regulation, energy capture, and clinical
integration.
Transcription:





                                                                             10

-   There are eight reactions in the Krebs cycle.
-    Luckily, you are not required to remember the enzymes in all of them. The slides
     will tell you which reactions you need to study.
-    Mostly, you should focus on the steps shown in red, which are the steps that
    regulate the Krebs cycle.
-   She also mentions step five, the reaction that produces GTP, and step six, the
     reaction that requires succinate dehydrogenase, because there is something
    unique about this enzyme.
-   The full cycle starts by combining acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
-   You are not required to remember any structures.
-  We go from a six-carbon molecule to a five-carbon molecule, then a four-carbon
    molecule, and come back to oxaloacetate.





                                                                             10

The first reaction of the TCA cycle is catalyzed by citrate synthase.
A 2-carbon acetyl group from acetyl-CoA combines with 4-carbon oxaloacetate,
producing 6-carbon citrate.
2C+4C=6C
This reaction is strongly favorable and is effectively irreversible under normal cellular
conditions.
Citrate synthase activity depends heavily on whether its two substrates, acetyl-CoA
and oxaloacetate, are available. This is particularly important because acetyl-CoA
cannot enter the cycle efficiently if oxaloacetate is depleted.
When citrate accumulates, this indicates that carbon and energy supply are relatively
abundant. Citrate can therefore help reduce further metabolic flux, including inhibition
of citrate synthase and inhibition of PFK-1 in glycolysis.
Key point: Acetyl-CoA cannot simply enter the TCA cycle alone; it must first combine
with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
Transcription:
-    Step one is important and is catalyzed by citrate synthase.
-    This is the entry step for acetyl-CoA into the Krebs cycle.
-     It is an irreversible reaction.
-   The flux of this reaction depends on how much acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate we





                                                                             11

-   have in the cell.
-      If there is an accumulation of citrate, this will inhibit this step.
-    Citrate accumulation signals abundant fuel and therefore inhibits PFK-1, which is
    the rate-limiting, committed, highly regulated step of glycolysis.





                                                                             11

Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes one of the most important regulatory reactions of
the TCA cycle.
The enzyme converts 6-carbon isocitrate into 5-carbon α-ketoglutarate. During the
reaction, one carbon is released as CO₂, and NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.
This is therefore an oxidative decarboxylation reaction.
The enzyme responds to the cell’s energy status. When energy demand is high, ADP
rises and stimulates the enzyme. In contracting muscle, increased Ca²⁺ also stimulates
TCA-cycle activity so that ATP production can increase.
In contrast, abundant ATP and NADH signal that energy supply is already sufficient and
inhibit the enzyme.
Key point: isocitrate dehydrogenase is a major flux-control point whose activity
changes according to cellular energy demand.
Transcription:
-    Reaction two, which converts citrate to isocitrate, is not important.
-    Reaction three is very important. We go from isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate.
-    Reaction three is a major control point of the Krebs cycle.
-     It is catalyzed by isocitrate dehydrogenase.
-  We go from six-carbon isocitrate to five-carbon alpha-ketoglutarate, and we
    produce NADH.





                                                                             12

-    This step is regulated by the energy level of the cell.
Regulation:
-     It is activated by low-energy signals and by increased calcium in contracting
    muscles.
-     It is inhibited by high ATP and high NADH.
-    This is similar to the regulation of the PDH reaction.





                                                                             12

α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase catalyzes the second oxidative decarboxylation of the
TCA cycle:
alpha Ketoglutarate (5C)  →   Succinyl-CoA (4C) + CO2
At the same time, NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.
This is an important flux-controlling step of the cycle. The enzyme responds to the
cell’s energy state:
ADP activates α-KGDH, supporting greater TCA-cycle flux when energy demand is high.
Ca²⁺ activates the complex, particularly in contracting muscle.
ATP and NADH inhibit the enzyme when the cell is in a high-energy state.
Succinyl-CoA, the reaction product, also inhibits the complex by feedback/product
inhibition.
Like PDH, α-KGDH is a multienzyme complex and uses the same five coenzymes: TPP,
lipoamide, CoA, FAD, and NAD⁺.
Key point: α-KGDH helps regulate TCA-cycle flux by integrating low-energy signals
(ADP, Ca²⁺) with high-energy/product signals (ATP, NADH, succinyl-CoA).
Transcription:
-    Step four is the second major control point.
-  We go from five-carbon alpha-ketoglutarate to four-carbon succinyl-CoA.
-   The enzyme alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is similarly regulated by the





                                                                             13

-   energy level.
-    In addition, it is controlled by its product.
-      If there is an accumulation of succinyl-CoA, this causes feedback inhibition, or
    product inhibition.
-    Therefore, succinyl-CoA inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
-    This is the second enzyme we see today that requires the five coenzymes
    described earlier. They are derived from B vitamins, except for lipoic acid.
Summary of the major control points:
-  We have seen the two major control points of the Krebs cycle: isocitrate
    dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
-   Both are regulated by the energy level of the cell.
-   The entry point, catalyzed by citrate synthase, is sensitive to the availability of
    acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. Citrate accumulation can also inhibit citrate
    synthase, but succinyl-CoA is the most important regulator of this step, according
    to the lecture.
-      If succinyl-CoA is accumulating, it means there is a buildup, so we cannot proceed
     in the Krebs cycle and stop from the beginning.
-    Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is inhibited by succinyl-CoA, its end product.
-    Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and PDH both require the five coenzymes.





                                                                             13

Succinyl-CoA synthetase converts 4-carbon succinyl-CoA into 4-carbon succinate.
The reaction uses energy stored in the high-energy thioester bond of succinyl-CoA to
form GTP from GDP and inorganic phosphate.
Because GTP is formed directly from a metabolic intermediate, this is called substrate-
level phosphorylation.
This is the only substrate-level phosphorylation reaction in the TCA cycle.
The distinction is important: GTP is generated directly here, whereas NADH and FADH₂
generate ATP later through oxidative phosphorylation.
Transcription:
-    Step five is the only substrate-level phosphorylation of the Krebs cycle.
-    This is the only reaction where you see the production of GTP.
-  We do not have an investment phase in the Krebs cycle, unlike glycolysis.
-   The purpose of the Krebs cycle is to produce energy, and it does not require an
    investment in energy.
-    Succinyl-CoA is converted to succinate, CoA is released, and GTP is produced.
-    Succinyl-CoA is a high-energy molecule capable of substrate-level
    phosphorylation.
-   She compares this to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) and
    phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) in glycolysis.





                                                                             14

Transcription:
-    In step six, we go from succinate to fumarate.
-    This step is important because it is catalyzed by succinate dehydrogenase.
-    Succinate dehydrogenase is a unique enzyme because it is part of both the Krebs
     cycle and the electron transport chain.
-     It is located in, and embedded in, the inner mitochondrial membrane.
-     It is part of Complex II of the electron transport chain.





                                                                             15

The TCA cycle is regulated mainly at three important control points:
citrate synthase
isocitrate dehydrogenase
α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
The overall principle is simple: when the cell needs more ATP, signals such as ADP and,
in contracting muscle, Ca²⁺ increase cycle activity.
When energy is already abundant, ATP and NADH inhibit key enzymes and reduce
TCA-cycle flux.
The cycle therefore responds continuously to the energy state of the cell rather than
running at a fixed rate.
Transcription:
-   The TCA cycle does not consume oxygen directly.
-   However, it generates NADH and FADH₂, and these must be reoxidized.
-   They are reoxidized in the electron transport chain, which requires oxygen.
-    Therefore, glycolysis and the TCA cycle require oxygen indirectly to regenerate the
     oxidized electron carriers.





                                                                             16

The TCA cycle does not contain a reaction in which oxygen is directly consumed.
Instead, oxygen is required at the level of the electron transport chain.
NADH and FADH₂ produced by the TCA cycle donate electrons to the ETC. Oxygen
accepts those electrons at the end of the chain and is reduced to water.
This allows NAD⁺ and FAD to be regenerated.
If oxygen is severely limited, the ETC slows, NADH accumulates, and NAD⁺ becomes
less available. Because several TCA-cycle reactions require NAD⁺, the cycle also slows.
Key point:
No oxygen used directly in the TCA cycle; oxygen is required indirectly to keep the
oxidized cofactors available.
Transcription:
-    Electron transport chain activity decreases, so there are not enough oxidized
    electron carriers.
-   As a result, the TCA cycle slows down.
-   Under hypoxic conditions, or if there is a problem with the electron transport
     chain, NADH accumulates and the Krebs cycle slows down.
-   The cell relies more on anaerobic glycolysis, leading to increased lactate
    production.





                                                                             17

The TCA cycle is described as amphibolic because it has both catabolic and anabolic
functions.
Its catabolic role is to oxidize acetyl-CoA and capture energy in NADH, FADH₂, and GTP.
Its anabolic role is to provide intermediates for synthesis of other molecules. For
example:
citrate can contribute to lipid synthesis
α-ketoglutarate can contribute to amino acid synthesis
succinyl-CoA contributes to heme synthesis
oxaloacetate can contribute to amino acid synthesis and gluconeogenesis
Because intermediates can leave the cycle for biosynthesis, the cell must also have
mechanisms to replace them. That leads directly to the next topic: anaplerosis.
Transcription:
-   A unique feature of the Krebs cycle is that it is amphibolic.
-   What do we mean by amphibolic? Although the main aim of the Krebs cycle is to
    produce energy, which makes it catabolic, the Krebs cycle is also anabolic.
-   Many of the intermediates of the Krebs cycle participate in different biosynthetic
    pathways.
-    Citrate is used for fatty acid synthesis and cholesterol synthesis.
-    Alpha-ketoglutarate can be changed into glutamate and other amino acids.





                                                                             18

-   Key message: although the kreb cycle is energy producing pathway it’s a source of
   many biosynthetic precursor and you’ll see it in the next lecture that oxaloacetate
      is also a source of glucose
-   Because the krebs cycle is very important for energy production and because
   some intermediates can be depleted, how can we avoid this? We can avoid this by
    having reactions to replace those intermediates that are depleted





                                                                             18

Pyruvate carboxylase is a mitochondrial enzyme that converts 3-carbon pyruvate into
4-carbon oxaloacetate.
The reaction requires ATP and biotin and adds one carbon in the form of CO₂.
Its main role in this context is anaplerotic: it replenishes oxaloacetate when TCA-cycle
intermediates have been withdrawn for biosynthesis.
Oxaloacetate is also important for gluconeogenesis, so this reaction connects the TCA
cycle with glucose production.
Pyruvate carboxylase is activated by acetyl-CoA. This makes metabolic sense because
when acetyl-CoA accumulates, the cell needs sufficient oxaloacetate available to
combine with it and sustain TCA-cycle activity.
Key distinction:
PDH: pyruvate → acetyl-CoA
Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate → oxaloacetate
Transcription:
-   One example is that if oxaloacetate of the Krebs cycle is depleted because it is
    converted to glucose, one reaction that replaces that oxaloacetate is the reaction
    catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.
-    Pyruvate carboxylase will change pyruvate, the three-carbon pyruvate, into four-
    carbon oxaloacetate.





                                                                             19

-  We are not going to study the reaction in detail because you are going to study it
     in detail later.
-    Pyruvate carboxylase is an example of what we call an anaplerotic reaction.
-   What do we mean by an anaplerotic reaction? It's a reaction that replenishes the
    intermediates of the Krebs cycle.
-    Pyruvate carboxylase requires ATP, biotin, and CO₂. That's why we refer to it as
   ABC carboxylase.
-    This reaction is not part of the Krebs cycle. It's a reaction that ensures that we
    always have oxaloacetate. The reaction is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.





                                                                             19

The TCA cycle is the central mitochondrial pathway that oxidizes acetyl-CoA while
capturing energy mainly as NADH and FADH₂.
Its activity is regulated according to cellular energy demand, especially at citrate
synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
The cycle is also amphibolic, because its intermediates are used in biosynthetic
pathways. When those intermediates are removed, anaplerotic reactions replenish
them, especially the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase.
Key point: the TCA cycle is not simply an energy-producing loop; it is a major
metabolic hub connecting catabolism, biosynthesis, and cellular energy status.
